extracted.intended_audience: natural philosophers, anatomists, and experimental scientists (readers/contributors to the Philosophical Transactions / Royal Society)
extracted.subtask_short: anatomical description and experimental natural history
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and exemplars for conducting and reporting dissections, anatomical description, functional experiments, and related experimental natural-history work (including mineral analysis and physiological/mechanical inference). Emphasises careful method, figures, measurements, comparative inference, and engagement with prior literature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crystallization for ascertaining saline contents
rubrics_metrics.description: The most rational way, in the opinion of this author, of ascertaining what the saline contents of the several waters in England are, is to crystallize them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This crystallization is to be done with great care and accuracy, not at once in a lump, but after many experiments, ablutions, dissolutions, and shootings, till you have the whole mass of salt fairly and singly crystallized. Then compare these crystals with the crystals of all the known fossile salts, and describe known salts from their fairest crystals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use labelled figures to illustrate anatomical descriptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Accompany descriptive prose with detailed, labelled figures (the 'Explanation of the Figures' accompanying each plate).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Figures should show parts opened or in situ (lungs, heart, gullet, stomach, teeth, skull, vertebrae, rattles, etc.), with lettered labels and a keyed explanation so that shape, size, and relative position are readily understood; the author credits Richard Waller's designs as crucial to illustrating what the pen could less easily describe.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct experimental manipulation to test function (with caution)
rubrics_metrics.description: Test functional hypotheses by direct manipulation and observation (e.g., pressing the gum caused poison to arise through the hollow of the fang).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such manipulations can reveal mechanics (the poison 'readily arose through the hollow of the tooth'), but invasive trials may destroy other evidence ('these trials spoiled our inquiry into the bags and glands'). Balance revealing tests against the risk of spoiling other investigations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infer function by comparative anatomy and mechanical necessity
rubrics_metrics.description: Deduce the use of structures by comparing across species and by considering mechanical constraints (e.g., absence of vesiculae seminales → long coitus; forked/hooked penes and aculei retain the male in the female).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use cross-species comparisons and attention to how parts are shaped, articulated, or positioned to argue functional roles (examples given: dogs, rattle-snake, vipers; maxillarum dilatores to enable swallowing large bodies).

rubrics_metrics.name: Describe microstructure and infer physiological function
rubrics_metrics.description: Give exact microscopic descriptions of tissues (e.g., muscle composed of bundles forming hexagonal/triangular prisms; fibers parallel; single fiber a cylinder full of spongy pith).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From microscopic structure infer function (the author 'asserts their proper action to be contraction'), critique prior theories modestly, and support claims with experiments and measurements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply quantitative mechanics to explain posture and locomotion
rubrics_metrics.description: Assign centres of gravity and compute force ratios to explain postures, standing, walking, leaping, flying, and swimming.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use numerical comparisons (e.g., vis motiva to weight as 2,900 to 1 for leaping; muscle potency exceeds bird weight 10,000 times) and trajectories (centre of gravity describes a parabola under oblique motion) to ground biomechanical claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: When proposing technological/engineering solutions, address practical problems empirically
rubrics_metrics.description: Designs (e.g., for diving apparatus or diving ships) must consider practical difficulties such as moist air fouling and propulsion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposed remedies include an air-pumping circulation through pipes to keep air untained, and mechanical propulsion ideas (a flexible spring oar imitating fish tails). Anticipate and solve identified practical objections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical criteria for evaluating reproductive hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate theories of generation by empirical plausibility, mechanical feasibility, reproducibility, and alternative explanations (e.g., Lewenhoek's animalcules vs. 'eggs' in the tuba).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Question claims that require improbable mechanics (how could pea-sized 'eggs' pass through very narrow tubes?), demand that phenomena should be reproducibly observed immediately after relevant events (e.g., 'always when searched for immediately after copulation'), and consider alternative causes (excretions, residua of semen).

rubrics_metrics.name: Record precise counts, measurements, colours, and note specimen variation
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide counts (e.g., scales, vertebrae, rattles), measurements, and colour descriptions, and note possible damage or variation in specimens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'from the neck to the anus there were ... 168 [scales], from the anus to the rattle 29 more'; rattles noted as hollow, brittle, sonorous; some rattles possibly broken off. Such particulars support comparative claims and life-history inferences (e.g., alleged annual addition of a new rattle).

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge prior literature and collaborators; consult literature to fill gaps
rubrics_metrics.description: When direct observation is incomplete or destroyed, rely on and cite prior relevant works (e.g., Charas, Redi, Grew) and acknowledge assistance (e.g., Richard Waller) and specimen repositories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly cite prior authors to supply missing facts ('our defect therein may be well supplied with what Charas and Redi have written'), acknowledge artists and preparers, and indicate where specimens are deposited (Royal Society repository).
